f80282cc7f701ecb.text: Make it yours. You'll read websites, reports and textbooks for assignments, at TAFE and at work. Using what you read is fine — copying it and pretending it's yours is not. That's plagiarism. Plagiarism includes copying a website, a friend's work or text from an AI tool and handing it in as your own. Changing a few words doesn't fix it. In VCE, work that can't be shown to be yours is treated as a breach of the rules. At work, it can cost you your job. There are three honest moves: Notes. Write key words, not whole sentences. Notes help you remember without copying. Paraphrase. Read it, cover it, say it out loud in your own way, then write it down. Check you kept the meaning. Summarise. Give just the main idea in fewer words. Ask: what's the one thing this is saying? If you use someone's exact words, put them in quotation marks. And always acknowledge your source: “According to the Fair Work Ombudsman, …”

e7d08b8f9f47a2b0.text: The speech that copied. In July 2016, Melania Trump gave a big speech in the United States. Within hours, people noticed something. Some parts were almost the same as a speech Michelle Obama gave in 2008. Two days later, a speechwriter called Meredith McIver said it was her mistake. Melania had read her parts of Michelle Obama's speech as examples. McIver wrote them into the draft. She didn't check them. She said sorry and offered to quit her job. It became one of the biggest stories of the week. But it was about the copying, not the speech. Think about it. What was copied, and how did it happen? What were the consequences? How could the speechwriter have avoided it?

80c474183695ad1b.text: VCAA's rules for your own work. The VCAA runs the VCE. That includes VCE VM. It has rules about work you hand in for school. Here are the main ones. The work you hand in must be your own. The rule says: “all unacknowledged work submitted is their own”. You must say where your information came from. That includes texts and websites. You can't get too much help from other people. That includes your teacher. So what is OK? You can use ideas from other places. But you must change them into your own work. What is not OK? Copying someone else's work. Copying a sample answer. What if the school can't tell that the work is yours? Then it counts as breaking the rules. Think about it. Who is this text written for, and why? Which kinds of help are OK, and which aren't?

5fd979ac6f90ca96.text: Make it yours. You'll read websites, reports and textbooks for assignments, at TAFE and at work. Using what you read is expected — presenting it as your own is plagiarism. Plagiarism includes copying a website, a friend's work or AI-generated text, and “patchwriting” — swapping a few words but keeping someone else's sentences. In VCE, VCAA's rules require that all unacknowledged work you submit is your own; work that can't be authenticated is treated as a breach of rules. In workplaces, plagiarism can end careers. The VCAA rules also say what is acceptable: using ideas from other sources that you've transformed and used in a new context. That's what these moves do: Notes. Key words, not sentences, so you're not tempted to copy. Paraphrase. Read, cover, say it your way, write, then check the meaning. Summarise. Reduce a text to its main idea and purpose. Use quotation marks for exact words, and acknowledge every source. Images and music are protected by copyright too: credit the creator and check you're allowed to use them.

fdf61efea6de4b22.text: VCAA's rules for your own work. The VCAA runs the VCE, including VCE VM. Its rules for school-based work include these: “a student must make sure that all unacknowledged work submitted is their own” a student must acknowledge all resources used, such as texts and websites a student must not get undue assistance. That means too much help, even from a teacher. The rules say some help is fine. You can use ideas from other sources if you have transformed them and used them in a new way. Copying someone's work or a sample answer is not fine. If any part of the work can't be shown to be yours, it is treated as a breach of rules. Think about it. Who is this text written for, and why? Which kinds of help are OK, and which aren't?
